newsitem.title: UK: Struggling dollar tries to find foothold in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Struggling dollar tries to find foothold in Europe.

text.p: The dollar was struggling to gain a foothold in early European trade after continuing to be knocked down overnight to its lowest level against the yen since late January.

Analysts said that while the outlook for the dollar was still positive in the medium term and that they did not expect a dollar plunge in European trade today, there was little at the moment to give the U.S. currency a sharp boost.
"It'll just try to steady today, although there is the risk is that we'll get another round of selling," said Lee Ferridge, currency strategist at Commerzbank in London.
The dollar has fallen about six yen since last Friday, hit by uncertainty over the outlook for U.S. and Japanese interest rates, which had been a major force behind the dollar's recent strength.

Dollar/yen hit a low of 117.50 in Tokyo overnight, according to data supplied by the Bank of Japan. Monday's slide was triggered by Eisuke Sakakibara, head of the Japanese Finance Ministry's international finance bureau, who said on Saturday the dollar's drop since Friday was "not overly excessive".
The dollar had recovered to 118.94/98 by 0746 GMT, although still below the 120.05/10 seen in late Friday European trade.
The dollar was also shaky against the mark in tandem with its drop against the yen, standing off its overnight highs at 1.6836/41 against its late Friday European level of 1.6863/68.
Dollar/yen was pulled off its lows by dollar-supportive comments by senior Japanese officials, who during the dollar's recent rally had been expressing their worries about the yen's weakness.
A senior official of Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party said a dollar/yen rate of around 120 would be the most appropriate level, and that he did not see the yen weakening for some time.
Taku Yamasaki, head of the LDP's policy research council, also said that changing Japan's record-low interest rates would undermine the economy.

"The Japanese officials are worried, they didn't want the dollar to suddenly collapse like this. All they wanted to do was stop the uptrend, they didn't want it to come back down as there's no benefit in Japan seeing a weaker dollar at the moment," Commerzbank's Ferridge said.
Analysts said, meanwhile, that expectations of a U.S. rate hike may not revive sufficiently to help the dollar unless U.S. data due this week are considerably stronger than expected.

"(U.S.) Price data is expected to be benign, and while we expect industrial production to be marginally stronger than the consensus, we expect retail sales to be softer," said Klaus Baader, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

"Coming in the week ahead of the FOMC, this is likely to further reduce expectations of a May Fed funds hike," Baader said. The Fed is due to hold its next policy-making Federal Open Market Committee meeting on May 20.
On the Japanese front, more data and further sustained strength in the Tokyo stock market was needed for expectations of a rate hike there to become more concrete, analysts said.

"A rate hike is possible in July. But we need data on the real economy since the tax hike (in April), and we need the Nikkei to move above 21,000, and we haven't got either of those yet," Commerzbank's Ferridge said.
The yen's strength pulled mark/yen down to its lowest level against the Japanese currency since May 31 last year. Mark/yen was at 70.42/45 against Friday's 71.42/47.

The mark was mixed on its European crosses, underpinned by dollar/mark's softness but stuck around late Friday levels. The British pound was a touch weaker against the mark and firmer on the dollar. -- Chizu Nomiyama, London Forex +44-171-542-6721
